title: Performance Measurement
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and terminology of Performance Measurement.
Apply or interpret one Express.js 5 pattern related to request duration metrics.
Identify a meaningful edge case and choose a repeatable local test for it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn performance measurement and connect the named syllabus points to a small Express.js example. The course baseline is Express 5.x on a supported Node.js LTS release; the page shows reference output, not execution of Node.js code.
content.why_it_matters: Performance Measurement matters because it helps keep the request/response contract explicit and the application maintainable as inputs, users and dependencies become less predictable. Measure before optimizing.

content_blocks.title: Concept map: Performance Measurement
content_blocks.alt_text: A conceptual three-stage flow for Performance Measurement: context or input, the Express.js concept, and verification of expected behavior with an edge case.
content_blocks.caption: Use this visual to connect request duration metrics to performance measurement; the final step is to verify both normal and boundary behavior.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Performance Measurement is part of performance, concurrency, and scalability. Node handles I/O asynchronously, but CPU-heavy work can block the event loop. Measure latency and error rates, limit work, tune data access, control cache freshness, and design backpressure and shutdown behavior. For this topic, make the observable behavior explicit, then check what happens when an input is missing, malformed, unauthorized, or a dependency fails (choose the relevant cases for this lesson).

items.title: Request duration metrics
items.text: Connect this syllabus point to Performance Measurement: state the expected behavior, identify a realistic edge case, and choose a test or observation that proves the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

items.title: Throughput and latency
items.text: Measure representative traffic first, then optimize the measured bottleneck. Cache only data with an explicit freshness/invalidation policy and bound results and concurrent work.

items.title: Error rates
items.text: Normalize expected failures into safe, predictable responses and forward unexpected failures to the final error handler. Keep diagnostic details in protected logs, not public responses.

items.title: Identifying slow routes
items.text: Treat the HTTP method and path as an API contract. Use the current Express 5 path syntax, validate captured values, and test both matching and non-matching requests.

items.title: Profiling before optimizing
items.text: Connect this syllabus point to Performance Measurement: state the expected behavior, identify a realistic edge case, and choose a test or observation that proves the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: Read the example carefully
content_blocks.text: A useful way to study performance measurement is to start from the first syllabus point — request duration metrics — and follow it through a small request or application example. Keep Express's built-in behavior separate from optional packages and your own application policy.

content_blocks.title: Worked example (reference only)
content_blocks.code:
const results = await Promise.all([loadA(), loadB()]);
res.set('Cache-Control', 'no-store').json({ results });

content.task: Try it yourself: adapt the worked example to demonstrate performance measurement. Write down the exact request or command, expected status/body, one boundary case, and how you would reset the local lab. CodeLeaf does not execute Express code in this lesson page; run Node.js server examples locally.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example has a clear local run or inspection path and the required dependencies are named.
A normal request and a malformed/edge/failure request have documented expected outcomes.
No credentials, production data, or claim of successful runtime execution is included.
hints: Hint 1: identify which part of performance measurement is supplied by Express and which part belongs to your own application or another package.
Hint 2: check the official Express 5 guide/API reference and isolate the smallest example that proves one behavior.
Hint 3: verify a success case, a boundary case and the expected status/response; restart from a clean state before repeating.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: Node handles I/O asynchronously, but CPU-heavy work can block the event loop. Measure latency and error rates, limit work, tune data access, control cache freshness, and design backpressure and shutdown behavior. The sample is a focused reference fragment. Review all dependency, schema, proxy and runtime assumptions before using it in an application.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying an example without checking its assumptions
common_mistakes.why: A fragment may omit route setup, middleware order, external packages, database schema or production configuration.
common_mistakes.fix: State the runtime/dependency assumptions, run the focused example locally, and test a success path plus one failure path.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating all request values as trusted
common_mistakes.why: Parameters, query values, body properties, files and upstream responses can be missing or malicious.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate schema, type and bounds at the boundary; keep authorization and database constraints as separate checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the demo output means the server executed
common_mistakes.why: The course page shows reference output for Node.js/Express code; it is not an isolated Node runtime.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the example locally with the documented Node.js version and record actual command/output and test results.

summary: Explain the central idea behind performance measurement.
Connect the relevant subtopics to the request/response or application boundary.
Verify one normal outcome and one edge/error case with repeatable evidence.
run_instructions: Open a terminal in the lesson lab directory.
Install dependencies for the sample if required; use a supported Node.js LTS release.
Run the documented file with node, send the stated request with curl or an API client, and compare the actual status/body with the reference.
reset_steps: Stop the local process with Ctrl+C.
Clear only temporary/synthetic records or files created by the lab.
Restart the server before repeating the example.
troubleshooting: If node reports a module-syntax error, check package.json module type or use the matching CommonJS syntax.
If a package cannot be resolved, install the named dependency in the local lab and verify the lockfile.
If output differs, verify middleware order, the request path/method, environment variables and the expected runtime version.
